questions.q: What is the primary function of the human nervous system?
a: To coordinate and control body responses to internal and external changes using electrical impulses
To pump blood through body tissues
To digest food molecules into nutrients
To filter urea from blood plasma

questions.q: Which two main organs make up the central nervous system (CNS) in humans?
What specialized cell type is responsible for transmitting electrical nerve impulses around the body?
Which type of neurone carries electrical impulses away from the central nervous system to effectors such as muscles or glands?
What is the name of the fatty insulating sheath that surrounds and protects many axons, speeding up nerve impulse transmission?
Which structures branch out from a neurone cell body to receive incoming electrical or chemical signals from other neurones?
What is the junction or microscopic gap between two adjacent neurones where chemical neurotransmitters transmit the signal?
How is a nerve impulse transmitted across a chemical synapse from one neurone to the next?
a: By direct electrical sparking across the gap
By physical movement of whole cell nuclei
By rapid diffusion of mineral ions only
By release of neurotransmitter chemical molecules that diffuse across the gap and bind to receptor proteins

questions.q: What is a reflex action?
a: A rapid, automatic, involuntary response to a stimulus that bypasses conscious brain control to protect the body
A slow, learned behavior practiced over many years
A conscious decision made during problem-solving
A hormonal response regulating blood sugar

questions.q: What is the correct sequence of components in a reflex arc?
a: Effector -> Motor neurone -> CNS -> Sensory neurone -> Receptor
Receptor -> Sensory neurone -> Relay neurone (CNS) -> Motor neurone -> Effector

questions.q: What is the role of a receptor in the nervous system?
a: To detect specific stimuli (changes in the environment) and convert them into electrical impulses

questions.q: Which component in a reflex arc carries out the final response, such as a muscle contracting or a gland secreting a substance?
What part of the central nervous system coordinates complex balance, posture, and fine muscular coordination?
Which part of the brain controls unconscious vital activities such as heart rate, breathing rate, and blood pressure?
What is the main difference between nervous coordination and hormonal (endocrine) coordination?
a: Hormonal responses are electrical impulses traveling along nerves
Nervous responses are fast-acting and short-lived, whereas hormonal responses are slower and longer-lasting

questions.q: What are chemical messengers produced by endocrine glands and transported in the blood plasma called?
Which endocrine gland is known as the 'master gland' because it secretes several hormones that control other glands in the body?
Which hormone is released by the adrenal glands during stressful, frightening, or exciting situations to prepare the body for 'fight or flight'?
What physical effects does adrenaline have on the body during an emergency response?
a: It slows the heart rate and constricts pupils
It stops breathing and digests food
It increases heart rate, dilates pupils, and redirects blood flow to skeletal muscles

questions.q: What is the name of the light-sensitive layer at the back of the human eye containing receptor cells (rods and cones)?
What is the function of the iris in the human eye?
a: To control the size of the pupil and regulate the amount of light entering the eye
To focus light onto the retina
To bend light rays entering the eye
To provide blood supply to the eyeball

questions.q: What happens to the circular and radial muscles of the iris when moving from a bright room into a dark room?
a: Circular muscles contract to make the pupil very small
Radial muscles contract, causing the pupil to dilate (widens) to let in more light

questions.q: What term describes the eye's ability to change the shape of the lens to focus clearly on near or distant objects?
How does the eye focus on a near object (accommodation)?
a: Ciliary muscles relax, suspensory ligaments pull tight, and the lens becomes thin
Ciliary muscles contract, suspensory ligaments slacken (loosen), and the lens becomes thicker and more curved
The iris removes the lens completely

questions.q: What type of photoreceptor cells in the retina are responsible for color vision and function best in bright light?
Which photoreceptor cells are extremely sensitive to dim light (allowing night vision) but do not detect color?
What is the chemical substance produced by the pancreas that lowers blood glucose levels by converting excess glucose into glycogen?
What metabolic condition occurs when a person's pancreas fails to produce sufficient insulin, leading to dangerously high blood glucose levels?
What is homeostasis?
a: The maintenance of a constant, stable internal environment within the body despite external changes
The uncontrolled growth of body tissues
The breakdown of food in the gut

questions.q: Which part of the brain acts as the body's thermostat, monitoring and regulating core body temperature and water balance?
How does the human body respond to a rise in internal core temperature (e.g., during hard exercise or hot weather)?
a: Sweating and vasodilation of skin blood vessels to lose heat

questions.q: What physiological response occurs when the body gets too cold to reduce heat loss from the skin?
a: Blood vessels in the skin dilate wide
Hairs lie flat against the skin
Vasoconstriction of skin arterioles and shivering (muscles contracting rapidly)

questions.q: Which neurone carries signals from sensory receptors toward the central nervous system?
What is the transparent front outer layer of the eye that refracts (bends) light entering the eye?
What is the blind spot of the eye where the optic nerve leaves the retina?
a: The point where no receptor cells are present

questions.q: Which hormone is secreted by the thyroid gland to control the basal metabolic rate (the speed at which chemical reactions occur)?
